title: Heterogeneous tool orchestrator — output assertion and adaptive loop limiter
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Problem: Multi-tool chains (LLM -> tool A -> tool B -> LLM) expose production apps to several classes of risk: silent schema drift in tool outputs, runaway recursion when tools re-invoke the orchestrator, and unexplained latency spikes from heterogenous tool runtimes. We need an orchestrator layer that asserts structured outputs, applies compatibility normalization across tool versions, and enforces an adaptive loop limiter (backoff + circuit-breaker) while preserving streaming semantics and tool/function calling ergonomics.

Goal: Implement a Heterogeneous Tool Orchestrator prototype that: 1) validates and normalizes tool outputs against declared schemas, 2) injects sanitized results into downstream tools/LLM prompts with provenance metadata, 3) detects and mitigates recursion/loop patterns using adaptive limits and escape hatches, and 4) maintains low-latency streaming behavior for end-to-end responses.

This ticket covers design, implementation, tests, and a canary rollout for runtime and console integrations.
acceptance_criteria: Orchestrator enforces output schema assertions for registered tools and rejects or auto-normalizes mismatched outputs with a configurable policy (reject / coerce / warn).
Result injection metadata is attached to downstream calls: origin_tool, output_schema_version, and a compact provenance token — visible in tracing and logs.

Adaptive loop limiter prevents more than N chained re-invocations per request (configurable baseline), ramps down with exponential backoff, and triggers a circuit-open state with clear diagnostic reason codes.
Streaming responses remain compatible: partial tool results can be streamed to clients while still subject to schema assertions and backpressure control.
Compatibility layer can map legacy tool output keys to canonical structured output for the orchestrator to use (mapping rules loaded from config).
Unit and integration tests covering recursion scenarios, schema mismatch cases, streaming under throttling, and cross-version tool compatibility pass in CI.
Canary rollout (5% of traffic) shows no regression in p95 latency and <0.1% increase in error-rate for affected routes over a 48h window.
Telemetry exists for: loop depth histogram, circuit breaker open rate, schema-coercion count, normalized fields per-tool, and injected-provenance counts.
design_decisions: Use a declarative per-tool contract: JSON Schema + version identifier. This keeps runtime checks fast and cacheable.
Support three mismatch policies: reject (fail fast), coerce (best-effort normalized output), warn-only (log and continue) — default to coerce for user-facing hosted API routes.
Provenance token is a short base64 blob containing tool_key:version:trace_id:sequence, signed by runtime with a stable HMAC key for authenticity (rotated via KMS integration).

Adaptive loop limiter: hybrid approach using request-scoped loop counter + distributed short-lived token. Allow initial retry budget (2 calls), then exponential backoff with per-tenant caps. Circuit breaker threshold based on error-types (recursive-call, schema-failure, latency).

Streaming semantics: buffer and validate tool-chunks in a bounded streaming buffer. Emit validated chunks to client; if validation fails mid-stream, emit structured error event rather than closing silently.
Compatibility layer implemented as pluggable mappers (scripted lightweight transforms) loaded from config to avoid code deploys for simple key remaps and renames.
tradeoffs: Schema checks add CPU overhead; to mitigate, we compile schemas and reuse validators per worker and only validate changed fields for incremental streaming chunks.
Coercion risks masking bugs vs reject policy which surfaces problems early. We default to coerce for user experience but surface telemetry/alerts to detect latent issues.
Provenance tokens increase payload size slightly; we keep token compact and optional per route to control overhead.
Tighter loop limits reduce risk but may break complex legitimate workflows (e.g., multi-hop planners). Provide per-project overrides and a bail-out API for verified flows.

Gradual ramp: 5% -> 25% -> 100% with 24h wait and rollback conditions defined
Provide opt-out per-route via route config flag and per-tenant override via billing tier
